coach_says: Qxd5+ gives check, but the pawn on d5 was guarded by the queen on b3 along the b3-c4-d5 diagonal, so Qxd5 simply wins your queen for a pawn. A check is not a safe move by itself: before you capture, ask what defends the piece you are taking. Here a quiet move like Nf5 or Ra6 kept the balance.
also: check doesn't make a capture safe

coach_says: Your knight on f3 is pinned to the queen by the bishop on g4, and Black's knight is ready to jump to d4 to pile on it. After d3 Nd4, Black threatens Nxf3+ gxf3 Bh3, wrecking your king's pawns and winning the exchange on f1. Deal with the pin first: c3 takes d4 away from the knight, or h3 asks the bishop to decide.
also: take d4 away from the knight

coach_says: A c-pawn on the 7th can draw against a queen thanks to stalemate, but only if your king goes to the corner: with your king on a8, Qxc7 would be stalemate, so Black can never win a tempo to bring the king closer. Kc8 stepped in front of your own pawn, which gave Black the free move Ke6 and then Qd7 is mate. Remember: with a bishop's or rook's pawn on the 7th, head for the corner, never in front of the pawn.

Be5 put your bishop on a square where f3-f4 kicks it with tempo, and that push also lets White untangle the doubled f-pawns and bring the queen to f3. You were better because White's kingside is broken and your knight on d4 is strong; keep that by gaining time instead of giving it, for example a4, which drives the bishop to a2 where it is out of play, then bring the knight to f5 and h4 against the king.
concept: bishop kicked by a pawn with tempo
also: drive back the bishop with a4

coach_says: Against the Elephant Gambit the direct answer is exd5, taking the pawn and leaving Black's e5 pawn under fire from your knight. Nc3 lets Black play ...d4, hitting the knight so it has to retreat, and Black gains space for free. When your opponent offers a pawn in the centre, check whether taking it is safe before developing a piece where a pawn can chase it.

Bxc2 grabbed a second pawn, but it sent your bishop to c2 where nothing defends it. White answered with Bd7+ and Ba4, attacking the loose bishop and keeping your king boxed in, and you ended up giving material back. When you are already a pawn up in an endgame, retreat calmly (Bg6 or Bf5) and keep your pieces protected instead of chasing more pawns.

You are a pawn up and White's queenside pawns on a3 and b4 are loose while White's pieces sit at home. a5 hits b4 three times (pawn, queen and the f8 bishop) and opens the a-file against the white rook. Bd7 was a slow developing move that gave White time for Bd3, trading off your strong knight on f5. When the opponent is behind in development, strike at the weak pawns at once.

Count before you recapture: after cxd4 your pawn on d4 is attacked three times (knights on c6 and f5, queen on b6) and defended only twice (Nf3 and Qd1), so Black just wins it. Bd3 first would trade off the f5 knight, one of the attackers, and then cxd4 holds. Before recapturing in the centre, count attackers and defenders on that square.

White's h-pawn has a free run up the board, and with the bishops supporting it, it is White's main winning chance. c5 ignored it, so White can push h4 and h5 at once. Rh5 attacks the undefended h2 pawn and ties White's king to defending it. In endgames, deal with the opponent's most dangerous pawn before making your own plans.

Rd4 attacks the bishop, but it just steps back to g6 and you are still a pawn down, now with c2 hanging. Rd2 was better: it guards c2 and prepares Rd7, putting your rook on the seventh rank to attack f7 and c7, while Bxa7 is also threatened. When you have the only open file, use it to get your rook to the seventh rather than chasing a piece that can simply move.
also: chasing a piece that just retreats

coach_says: f6 is a reasonable way to kick the strong knight on e5; White can take the c6 pawn, but your active pieces give you enough for it. Nd6 was about as good. Nothing to fix here.
Both recaptures on d6 are about the same; cxd6 kept the e5 pawn cramping Black, but the real problem came earlier when you lost a piece. Recapturing here was fine.
Kxe7 is the best move: you remove the dangerous pawn on e7 before it can promote. Good.
The position was already lost: Black is a bishop up with connected passed pawns, so it is lost whatever you play. Be6 doesn't change that.
Kb3 is as good as anything; Black's extra bishop and the pawns on a3, b4 and h4 are too much, and the game was lost before this move.
Bxd3 is the best move: it trades off White's good attacking bishop and keeps your extra pawn. Well played.

Taking on c5 pulled your rook off the back rank, and your king on h8 has no escape square. White replies Qf7, threatening Qf8+ Rxf8 Rxf8 mate, so you have to go back with Rcc8 and White's e-pawn runs to e6 and e7. Rf8 was the move: it covers the back rank and challenges the queen and rook on the f-file. Before grabbing a pawn with a back-rank piece, check that your king still has cover.
